name: QuickBASIC
title: QuickBASIC on DOS
intro: QuickBASIC (and its free little sibling QBasic, which came with MS-DOS 5 and Windows 95) gave BASIC a full-screen editor, structured loops and named subroutines, so line numbers became optional. It is a good way to see how programs worked before windows and mice, and a gentle first language in its own right. To try it today, run QBasic or QuickBASIC 4.5 inside DOSBox, or use QB64, a modern compiler that understands the same code. Press F5 in the editor to run a program. Every example here shows exactly what it prints.

lessons.title: PRINT and the screen
lessons.summary: Showing text and numbers, and how PRINT spaces them.

sections.p: PRINT writes a line to the screen and CLS clears it. A comment starts with an apostrophe (or the older REM). PRINT on its own prints an empty line.
sections.code:
CLS
' My first program
PRINT "Hello from QuickBASIC"
PRINT
PRINT 6 * 7

sections.p: QuickBASIC prints a number with a space in front (where a minus sign would go) and one after. A negative number uses that front space for its minus sign. Text is printed exactly as written.
sections.code:
PRINT 5
PRINT -5
PRINT "5"

sections.p: A semicolon between items keeps the cursor on the same line; a comma jumps to the next 14-character column, which lines things up like a table. A semicolon at the very end means the next PRINT carries on the same line.
sections.code:
PRINT "Total:"; 5
PRINT "A", "B", "C"
PRINT "same ";
PRINT "line"
sections.out:
Total: 5
A             B             C
same line

sections.p: TAB(n) moves to column n of the line (counting from 1) and SPC(n) prints n spaces. They only work inside PRINT.
sections.code:
PRINT "Name"; TAB(10); "Nuts"
PRINT "Hazel"; TAB(10); "12"
PRINT "x"; SPC(3); "y"

practice.why: A semicolon joins items with nothing between them. Only numbers get their own padding spaces.
An apostrophe (or REM) starts a comment in QuickBASIC.
The sum is printed with the leading space QuickBASIC leaves for a sign.
The semicolon at the end keeps the cursor on the line, so the next PRINT carries on.
The space before a number is where its sign goes, so a negative number fills it with the minus.

practice.q: What does a comma between PRINT items do?
options: Joins the items with no space
practice.why: Commas line output up in print zones, which is handy for tables.
A comma jumps to the next 14-character print zone.
PRINT alone writes a blank line.

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.summary: Type suffixes, DIM ... AS, CONST and joining text.

sections.p: A variable is a name for a value. = stores a value in it (the old keyword LET is optional). The last character of a name sets its type: $ for text, % for a whole number, & for a long whole number, and ! or nothing for a decimal number.
sections.code:
who$ = "Hazel"
nuts% = 12
weight = 0.5
PRINT who$; " has"; nuts%; "nuts"
PRINT "and weighs"; weight; "kg"
sections.out:
Hazel has 12 nuts
and weighs .5 kg

sections.p: Notice .5 above: QuickBASIC leaves out the 0 before a decimal point. A variable that has never been given a value is 0, or an empty string for text.
sections.code:
PRINT never
PRINT "["; empty$; "]"

sections.p: Storing a decimal in a % variable rounds it to the nearest whole number. An INTEGER holds −32768 to 32767; a LONG (&) holds about ±2 billion.
sections.code:
a% = 7.6
b% = 7.2
PRINT a%; b%

sections.p: Instead of a suffix you can declare a type with DIM name AS type. The types are INTEGER, LONG, SINGLE, DOUBLE (more digits) and STRING.
sections.code:
DIM pet AS STRING
DIM legs AS INTEGER
pet = "squirrel"
legs = 4
PRINT "A "; pet; " has"; legs; "legs"

sections.p: + joins two strings. CONST names a value that never changes, which keeps magic numbers out of the program.
sections.code:
CONST TREES = 3
first$ = "Oak"
whole$ = first$ + " tree"
PRINT whole$; " x"; TREES

practice.why: The $ suffix makes a string variable.
A % variable holds whole numbers, so 4.7 is rounded to 5.
QuickBASIC drops the 0 in front of the decimal point.
+ joins strings in the order written.

practice.q: What is in count% if the program never set it?
practice.why: Number variables start at 0 and strings start empty.

practice.q: Which type holds the most digits?
practice.why: DOUBLE is double precision: about 15 digits against SINGLE's 7.
CONST N is a number, so PRINT leaves a space for its sign.

practice.code:
DIM n AS INTEGER
n = 2.9
PRINT n
practice.why: INTEGER stores whole numbers, so 2.9 rounds to 3.

lessons.title: Maths
lessons.summary: Operators, whole-number division, powers and the maths functions.

sections.p: + - * / work as on a calculator, and ^ raises to a power. \ (backslash) divides and drops the remainder; MOD gives the remainder.
sections.code:
PRINT 7 / 2
PRINT 7 \ 2
PRINT 7 MOD 2
PRINT 2 ^ 10

sections.p: Powers first, then a minus sign in front, then * and /, then \, then MOD, then + and -. Brackets go first of all.
sections.code:
PRINT 2 + 3 * 4
PRINT (2 + 3) * 4
PRINT 10 - 4 - 3

sections.p: Ordinary decimal variables are SINGLE precision, so PRINT shows at most 7 digits.
sections.code:
PRINT 10 / 3
PRINT 1 / 8

sections.p: INT rounds down to a whole number, FIX just chops off the decimals (they differ for negative numbers), ABS drops the sign and SQR is the square root.
sections.code:
PRINT INT(3.7); FIX(3.7)
PRINT INT(-3.7); FIX(-3.7)
PRINT ABS(-8); SQR(81)

sections.p: To change a variable, work out the new value from the old one and store it back.
sections.code:
score = 10
score = score + 5
score = score * 2
PRINT score

practice.why: Backslash is whole-number division: 5 fits into 17 three times.
17 is 3 × 5 with 2 left over.
Multiplication comes before addition: 2 × 3 = 6, then 1 + 6.
^ is a power: 3 squared.
INT always rounds down, and down from −1.5 is −2. FIX would give −1.
/ gives a decimal answer, printed without the leading 0.
FIX chops towards zero; INT would give −2.

practice.code:
s = 5
s = s * 3
s = s - 1
PRINT s
practice.why: 5 × 3 is 15, then subtract 1.

lessons.title: Working with text
lessons.summary: LEN, LEFT$, RIGHT$, MID$, INSTR, UCASE$, STR$, VAL, CHR$ and ASC.

sections.p: Functions whose names end in $ give back text. LEN counts characters. LEFT$ and RIGHT$ take characters from either end, and MID$(s$, start, length) takes them from the middle, counting from 1.
sections.code:
w$ = "squirrel"
PRINT LEN(w$)
PRINT LEFT$(w$, 3)
PRINT RIGHT$(w$, 3)
PRINT MID$(w$, 3, 4)

sections.p: INSTR(s$, find$) gives the position where find$ first appears, or 0 if it does not. UCASE$ and LCASE$ change case.
sections.code:
PRINT INSTR("hazelnut", "nut")
PRINT INSTR("hazelnut", "pea")
PRINT UCASE$("acorn"); " "; LCASE$("OAK")

sections.p: STR$ turns a number into text (keeping the space for the sign) and VAL turns text into a number, reading as far as it can. You cannot add a number to a string without converting it first.
sections.code:
n = 42
t$ = "Answer:" + STR$(n)
PRINT t$
PRINT VAL("12 apples") + 1

sections.p: Every character has a code number. ASC gives the code of the first character and CHR$ turns a code back into a character. Letters are in order, so adding to a code moves along the alphabet.
sections.code:
PRINT ASC("A")
PRINT CHR$(66)
PRINT CHR$(ASC("a") + 2)

sections.p: Strings compare letter by letter by their codes, so "apple" < "banana" is true. Every capital letter comes before every small letter, which is why programs often UCASE$ both sides first.
sections.code:
IF "apple" < "banana" THEN PRINT "apple first"
IF "Zebra" < "apple" THEN PRINT "capitals first"

practice.why: LEFT$ takes characters from the start.
Counting from 1, position 6 is n, and three characters are n, u, t.
The space counts as a character too.
w is 1, a is 2, l is 3.

options: Stops with a type mismatch error
practice.answer: Stops with a type mismatch error
practice.why: + cannot join text and a number; convert with STR$ first.
B is code 66; one more is 67, which is C.
RIGHT$ takes characters from the end.
VAL reads the leading number and stops at k.

lessons.title: Decisions
lessons.summary: IF, ELSEIF, ELSE, AND, OR, NOT and what true really is.

sections.p: Block IF runs lines until END IF. ELSEIF and ELSE add more branches; only the first matching one runs. Equality is a single =; not-equal is <>.
sections.code:
temp = 4
IF temp < 0 THEN
    PRINT "Freezing"
ELSEIF temp < 10 THEN
    PRINT "Chilly"
ELSE
    PRINT "Mild"
END IF

sections.p: For something short, put it all on one line. No END IF is needed. A colon separates several statements on one line.
sections.code:
nuts = 0
IF nuts = 0 THEN PRINT "Hungry!": PRINT "Off to find nuts"
IF nuts > 5 THEN PRINT "Full" ELSE PRINT "Not full"
sections.out:
Hungry!
Off to find nuts
Not full

sections.p: Combine tests with AND (both true), OR (at least one true) and NOT.
sections.code:
age = 12
IF age >= 10 AND age <= 19 THEN PRINT "Teenager or nearly"
IF age < 5 OR age > 65 THEN PRINT "Free entry" ELSE PRINT "Pay at the gate"
sections.out:
Teenager or nearly
Pay at the gate

sections.p: A comparison is really a number: −1 for true and 0 for false. IF treats any value that is not 0 as true. That is why NOT 0 is −1.
sections.code:
PRINT 3 > 2; 3 < 2
PRINT NOT 0
flag = 5
IF flag THEN PRINT "non-zero counts as true"

practice.q: How do you write “not equal” in QuickBASIC?
practice.why: BASIC uses <> for not equal.
Block IF statements end with END IF, written as two words.

practice.code:
x = 15
IF x > 20 THEN
    PRINT "big"
ELSEIF x > 10 THEN
    PRINT "medium"
ELSEIF x > 5 THEN
    PRINT "small"
END IF
practice.why: Only the first branch whose test is true runs, even though x > 5 is also true.
A true comparison has the value −1 in QuickBASIC.

practice.code:
a = 3
IF a > 1 AND a < 3 THEN PRINT "in" ELSE PRINT "out"
practice.why: a < 3 is false when a is 3, and AND needs both to be true.
Any non-zero number counts as true; IF "" is a type mismatch, since IF wants a number.

practice.code:
n = 0
IF n = 0 THEN PRINT "zero": PRINT "done"
IF n > 0 THEN PRINT "pos"
practice.why: The colon runs both statements on the one-line IF; the second IF is false.
NOT flips bits: NOT 0 is −1 (true) and NOT −1 is 0 (false).

sections.p: Counts from a start to an end value, inclusive. STEP sets how much to add each time; a negative step counts down.
sections.code:
FOR i = 1 TO 10 STEP 3
    PRINT i;
NEXT i
PRINT
FOR i = 3 TO 1 STEP -1
    PRINT i;
NEXT i

sections.p: A loop and a running total add up a list of numbers. This finds 1 + 2 + … + 100.
sections.code:
total = 0
FOR n = 1 TO 100
    total = total + n
NEXT n
PRINT total

sections.p: Repeats while (or until) a condition holds. With the test at the top the body might never run; with the test at the bottom (LOOP UNTIL, LOOP WHILE) it always runs at least once.
sections.code:
stash = 1
DO WHILE stash < 20
    stash = stash * 3
LOOP
PRINT stash
n = 100
DO
    n = n + 1
LOOP UNTIL n > 5
PRINT n

sections.p: WHILE ... WEND is the older form of DO WHILE ... LOOP. You will see it in older listings.
sections.code:
n = 1
WHILE n < 100
    n = n * 2
WEND
PRINT n

sections.p: EXIT FOR and EXIT DO leave a loop early, for example as soon as an answer is found.
sections.code:
FOR n = 2 TO 100
    IF n * n > 50 THEN EXIT FOR
NEXT n
PRINT "First square over 50 is"; n; "squared"

sections.p: Each pass of the outer loop runs the whole inner loop. This prints a small times table.
sections.code:
FOR r = 1 TO 3
    FOR c = 1 TO 4
        PRINT r * c;
    NEXT c
    PRINT
NEXT r

practice.q: How many numbers does FOR i = 1 TO 10 STEP 3 … NEXT print?
practice.why: 1, 4, 7 and 10. The end value counts when it is reached exactly.

practice.q: FOR i = 5 TO 1 STEP -2 visits which values?
practice.why: A negative STEP counts down, and 1 is reached exactly.
Starting at 2 and adding 2 each time reaches 8 exactly.

practice.code:
n = 10
DO WHILE n < 5
    n = n + 1
LOOP
PRINT n
practice.why: The test is at the top and is false straight away, so the body never runs.

practice.code:
n = 10
DO
    n = n + 1
LOOP WHILE n < 5
PRINT n
practice.why: With the test at the bottom the body runs once before the test is checked.

practice.code:
t = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 4
    t = t + i
NEXT i
PRINT t

practice.why: A negative STEP counts down and reaches 1.

practice.code:
FOR n = 1 TO 10
    IF n * n > 20 THEN EXIT FOR
NEXT n
PRINT n
practice.why: 4² is 16, still ≤ 20; 5² is 25, so EXIT FOR leaves n at 5.

lessons.title: SELECT CASE
lessons.summary: Choosing by value, by range and by comparison.

sections.p: SELECT CASE picks one branch by value, which reads better than a long chain of IFs. CASE ELSE catches everything not listed. Only the first matching case runs.
sections.code:
k$ = "S"
SELECT CASE k$
    CASE "N": PRINT "North"
    CASE "S": PRINT "South"
    CASE ELSE: PRINT "Stay"
END SELECT

sections.p: A case can list several values separated by commas, give a range with TO, or compare with IS.
sections.code:
FOR n = 0 TO 12 STEP 4
    SELECT CASE n
        CASE 0
            PRINT n; "none"
        CASE 1, 2, 3
            PRINT n; "a few"
        CASE 4 TO 9
            PRINT n; "several"
        CASE IS >= 10
            PRINT n; "lots"
    END SELECT
NEXT n

sections.p: Cases can be strings. Comparing UCASE$ of the input means the user can type either case.
sections.code:
answer$ = "yes"
SELECT CASE UCASE$(answer$)
    CASE "Y", "YES"
        PRINT "Great!"
    CASE "N", "NO"
        PRINT "Maybe later."
    CASE ELSE
        PRINT "Please answer yes or no."
END SELECT

practice.code:
n = 7
SELECT CASE n
    CASE 1 TO 5: PRINT "low"
    CASE 6 TO 10: PRINT "mid"
    CASE ELSE: PRINT "high"
END SELECT
practice.why: 7 falls in the range 6 TO 10.

practice.code:
n = 50
SELECT CASE n
    CASE IS > 10: PRINT "over ten"
    CASE IS > 40: PRINT "over forty"
END SELECT
practice.why: Both cases match, but only the first matching case runs.

practice.q: How do you write a case for 3 or 5 or 7?
practice.why: A comma-separated list matches any of its values. 3 TO 7 would also match 4 and 6.

practice.q: What runs if no case matches and there is no CASE ELSE?
practice.why: The program just carries on after END SELECT.

practice.code:
k$ = "N"
SELECT CASE k$
    CASE "N", "n": PRINT "north"
    CASE "S": PRINT "south"
END SELECT
practice.why: A comma list matches any listed value; k$ is N.

practice.code:
n = 2
SELECT CASE n
    CASE 1, 2, 3: PRINT "few"
    CASE 2: PRINT "two"
END SELECT
practice.why: Only the first matching case runs.

lessons.title: Arrays and DATA
lessons.summary: Numbered lists of values, filling them from DATA, and tables.

sections.p: An array is a row of variables sharing one name, picked by a number in brackets. DIM nuts(1 TO 5) makes five of them, numbered 1 to 5. A loop is the natural way to visit every one.
sections.code:
DIM nuts(1 TO 5)
FOR i = 1 TO 5
    nuts(i) = i * 10
NEXT i
PRINT nuts(1); nuts(5)
total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 5
    total = total + nuts(i)
NEXT i
PRINT "Total:"; total

sections.p: DIM a(10) without TO makes elements 0 to 10: eleven of them. Using a number outside the range stops the program with “Subscript out of range”.
DATA lines hold values inside the program. READ takes the next one each time it runs, which is a tidy way to fill an array. RESTORE starts again from the first value.
sections.code:
DIM names$(1 TO 3), ages(1 TO 3)
FOR i = 1 TO 3
    READ names$(i), ages(i)
NEXT i
FOR i = 1 TO 3
    PRINT names$(i); " is"; ages(i)
NEXT i
DATA "Hazel", 3, "Bramble", 5, "Acorn", 1
sections.out:
Hazel is 3
Bramble is 5
Acorn is 1

sections.p: To find the largest value, keep the best so far and compare each element with it.
sections.code:
DIM s(1 TO 6)
FOR i = 1 TO 6: READ s(i): NEXT i
best = s(1)
FOR i = 2 TO 6
    IF s(i) > best THEN best = s(i)
NEXT i
PRINT "Best score:"; best
DATA 12, 40, 7, 33, 41, 9

sections.p: An array can have two numbers: rows and columns. SWAP exchanges two variables, handy for sorting.
sections.code:
DIM grid(1 TO 2, 1 TO 3)
FOR r = 1 TO 2
    FOR c = 1 TO 3
        grid(r, c) = r * 10 + c
    NEXT c
NEXT r
PRINT grid(2, 3)
x = 1: y = 2
SWAP x, y
PRINT x; y

practice.q: How many elements does DIM a(1 TO 4) make?
practice.why: Elements 1, 2, 3 and 4.

practice.q: How many elements does DIM a(4) make?
practice.why: Without TO the numbering starts at 0, so it is 0 to 4.

practice.code:
DIM v(1 TO 3)
FOR i = 1 TO 3
    v(i) = i * i
NEXT i
PRINT v(3) - v(2)
practice.why: v(3) is 9 and v(2) is 4.

practice.code:
READ a, b
READ c
PRINT a + b + c
DATA 1, 2, 3, 4
practice.why: READ takes values in order: a = 1, b = 2, c = 3. The 4 is never read.

practice.code:
READ x
RESTORE
READ y
PRINT x; y
DATA 7, 8
practice.why: RESTORE goes back to the first DATA value, so y reads 7 again.

practice.q: What does SWAP a, b do?
options: Exchanges the values of a and b
Makes a and b the same variable
practice.answer: Exchanges the values of a and b
practice.why: After SWAP, a holds what b held and b holds what a held.
DIM a(2) makes indexes 0 to 2; 1 × 4 = 4.

practice.code:
x = 3: y = 9
SWAP x, y
PRINT x; y
practice.why: SWAP exchanges the two values.

lessons.title: SUBs and FUNCTIONs
lessons.summary: Naming pieces of a program so you can reuse them.

sections.p: A SUB does a job; a FUNCTION returns a value by assigning to its own name. The editor stores each one on its own page (press F2 to list them) and adds a DECLARE line at the top for you.
sections.code:
DECLARE SUB Banner (t$)
DECLARE FUNCTION Square% (n%)

Banner "Squares"
PRINT Square%(9)

SUB Banner (t$)
    PRINT "== "; t$; " =="
END SUB

FUNCTION Square% (n%)
    Square% = n% * n%
END FUNCTION

sections.p: Arguments are passed by reference: if a SUB changes its parameter, the caller's variable changes too. Wrap an argument in brackets to pass a copy instead.
sections.code:
DECLARE SUB AddOne (x%)
n% = 1
AddOne n%
PRINT n%
AddOne (n%)
PRINT n%

SUB AddOne (x%)
    x% = x% + 1
END SUB

sections.p: Variables inside a SUB or FUNCTION are its own: a count inside is a different variable from a count outside. DIM SHARED in the main program makes a variable that every SUB can see.
sections.code:
DECLARE SUB Bump ()
DIM SHARED score
score = 10
count = 1
Bump
PRINT score; count

SUB Bump
    score = score + 5
    count = 99
END SUB

sections.p: CALL Name(arguments) is another way to run a SUB. With CALL the arguments go in brackets; without it they do not.
sections.code:
DECLARE SUB Stars (n%)
CALL Stars(3)
Stars 5

SUB Stars (n%)
    PRINT STRING$(n%, "*")
END SUB

sections.p: A FUNCTION may call itself, as long as some case stops it. The factorial of n is n × (n − 1) × … × 1.
sections.code:
DECLARE FUNCTION Fact& (n%)
PRINT Fact&(5)
PRINT Fact&(10)

FUNCTION Fact& (n%)
    IF n% <= 1 THEN
        Fact& = 1
    ELSE
        Fact& = n% * Fact&(n% - 1)
    END IF
END FUNCTION

practice.q: How does a FUNCTION return its value?
options: By assigning to its own name
practice.answer: By assigning to its own name
practice.why: Inside FUNCTION Square%, writing Square% = … sets the result.

practice.q: A SUB sets its parameter to 0. The caller passed n%. What happens to n%?
practice.why: Arguments are passed by reference unless you wrap them in brackets.

practice.q: Which key lists the SUBs and FUNCTIONs in the QuickBASIC editor?
practice.why: F2 opens the SUBs list; F5 runs the program; F1 is help.

practice.code:
DECLARE FUNCTION Twice (x)
PRINT Twice(Twice(3))

FUNCTION Twice (x)
    Twice = x * 2
END FUNCTION
practice.why: The inner call gives 6 and the outer call doubles that.

practice.code:
DECLARE SUB Zap (v)
a = 5
Zap a
PRINT a

SUB Zap (v)
    v = 0
END SUB
practice.why: a is passed by reference, so setting v changes a.

practice.code:
DECLARE SUB Change ()
x = 1
Change
PRINT x

SUB Change
    x = 2
END SUB
practice.why: The x inside the SUB is its own local variable; without DIM SHARED the main x is untouched.

practice.code:
DECLARE FUNCTION Triple (n)
PRINT Triple(4)

FUNCTION Triple (n)
    Triple = n * 3
END FUNCTION
practice.why: The FUNCTION assigns Triple = n * 3, so 4 × 3 = 12.

practice.code:
DECLARE SUB AddOne (x%)
n% = 4
AddOne (n%)
PRINT n%

SUB AddOne (x%)
    x% = x% + 1
END SUB
practice.why: Brackets pass a copy, so changing x% does not change n%.

lessons.title: Input, colour and chance
lessons.summary: INPUT, INKEY$, LOCATE, COLOR, RND and SLEEP for interactive programs.

sections.p: These statements make programs interactive. Their output depends on the person at the keyboard or on chance, so try them in QBasic, DOSBox or QB64 rather than reading a fixed answer. INPUT shows a prompt and waits for the user to type and press Enter. The value lands in the variable you name.
sections.code:
INPUT "What is your name"; n$
INPUT "How many acorns"; a%
PRINT "Hello, "; n$; ". Double that is"; a% * 2

sections.p: RND gives a random number from 0 up to (but not including) 1. Multiply and take INT to get a whole number in a range. RANDOMIZE TIMER seeds the generator from the clock, so each run is different.
sections.code:
RANDOMIZE TIMER
die = INT(RND * 6) + 1      ' 1 to 6
PRINT "You rolled"; die

sections.p: LOCATE row, column moves the cursor (the text screen is 25 rows by 80 columns). COLOR foreground, background picks from 16 colours (0 black, 1 blue, 2 green, 4 red, 14 yellow, 15 white).
sections.code:
CLS
COLOR 14, 1
LOCATE 12, 35
PRINT "Centre stage"
COLOR 7, 0

sections.p: INKEY$ returns the key being pressed right now, or an empty string, without waiting. A loop around it waits for any key; SLEEP pauses for a number of seconds.
sections.code:
PRINT "Press any key..."
DO
LOOP WHILE INKEY$ = ""
PRINT "Thanks!"
SLEEP 1

sections.p: Put together, these make a complete game. The loop keeps asking until the guess is right, and counts the tries.
sections.code:
RANDOMIZE TIMER
secret = INT(RND * 100) + 1
tries = 0
DO
    INPUT "Guess (1-100)"; g
    tries = tries + 1
    IF g < secret THEN PRINT "Higher!"
    IF g > secret THEN PRINT "Lower!"
LOOP UNTIL g = secret
PRINT "Got it in"; tries; "tries."

practice.q: Which expression gives a whole number from 1 to 6?
practice.why: RND * 6 is 0 up to 5.999…; INT makes it 0 to 5, and + 1 shifts it to 1 to 6.

options: So each run gives different random numbers
practice.answer: So each run gives different random numbers
practice.why: Without a seed, RND gives the same sequence every run.

practice.q: What does INKEY$ give when no key is pressed?
practice.why: INKEY$ never waits, which makes it useful in game loops.
Rows and columns both count from 1 at the top left.

practice.q: In the guessing game, why LOOP UNTIL g = secret at the bottom?
options: The player must guess at least once
INPUT only works in that kind of loop
practice.answer: The player must guess at least once
practice.why: A test at the bottom always runs the body once before checking.

options: Yellow text on a blue background
practice.answer: Yellow text on a blue background
practice.why: 14 is yellow and 1 is blue in the 16-colour text palette.

practice.q: How many columns does the default text screen have?
practice.why: The text screen is 25 rows by 80 columns.

lessons.title: Putting it together: FizzBuzz
lessons.summary: Loops, MOD, decisions and a FUNCTION in one program.

sections.p: FizzBuzz counts from 1, but says Fizz for multiples of 3, Buzz for multiples of 5 and FizzBuzz for both. n MOD 3 = 0 is true exactly when n divides by 3. Building the word up piece by piece avoids testing 15 separately.
sections.code:
FOR n = 1 TO 15
    w$ = ""
    IF n MOD 3 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Fizz"
    IF n MOD 5 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Buzz"
    IF w$ = "" THEN PRINT n ELSE PRINT w$
NEXT n
sections.out:
1
 2
Fizz
 4
Buzz
Fizz
 7
 8
Fizz
Buzz
 11
Fizz
 13
 14
FizzBuzz

sections.p: The numbers above keep PRINT's leading space. LTRIM$(STR$(n)) turns a number into text with no spaces, so everything lines up. Moving the rule into a FUNCTION gives it a name.
sections.code:
DECLARE FUNCTION Say$ (n%)
FOR i% = 1 TO 15
    PRINT Say$(i%); " ";
NEXT i%
PRINT

FUNCTION Say$ (n%)
    w$ = ""
    IF n% MOD 3 = 0 THEN w$ = "Fizz"
    IF n% MOD 5 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Buzz"
    IF w$ = "" THEN w$ = LTRIM$(STR$(n%))
    Say$ = w$
END FUNCTION
sections.out: 1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz

sections.p: You know enough QuickBASIC to write real programs. Good next steps: change FizzBuzz to count to 100; turn the guessing game into one where the computer guesses your number; draw with SCREEN 12, LINE and CIRCLE; or look through the GORILLA.BAS and NIBBLES.BAS games that came with QBasic, which use everything in this course.

practice.why: 12 MOD 3 is 0, so the comparison is true, which prints as −1.
STR$ gives " 7" and LTRIM$ removes the space in front.

practice.code:
FOR n = 9 TO 10
    w$ = ""
    IF n MOD 3 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Fizz"
    IF n MOD 5 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Buzz"
    PRINT w$
NEXT n
practice.why: 9 divides by 3 only, and 10 divides by 5 only.

practice.q: Why build w$ up instead of testing 15 first?
options: A multiple of both gets both words added
It is the only way in BASIC
practice.answer: A multiple of both gets both words added
practice.why: 15 passes both tests, so Fizz and then Buzz are added and FizzBuzz comes out.

practice.code:
FOR n = 14 TO 15
    w$ = ""
    IF n MOD 3 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Fizz"
    IF n MOD 5 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Buzz"
    IF w$ = "" THEN PRINT n ELSE PRINT w$
NEXT n
practice.why: 14 is neither multiple; 15 is both, so Fizz then Buzz are joined.

practice.code:
DECLARE FUNCTION Say$ (n%)
PRINT Say$(6); ","; Say$(10)

FUNCTION Say$ (n%)
    w$ = ""
    IF n% MOD 3 = 0 THEN w$ = "Fizz"
    IF n% MOD 5 = 0 THEN w$ = w$ + "Buzz"
    IF w$ = "" THEN w$ = LTRIM$(STR$(n%))
    Say$ = w$
END FUNCTION
practice.why: 6 is only a multiple of 3; 10 is only a multiple of 5.
